provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of primary five work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to recall primary five English concepts.
The pupils should be able to complete a reading and writing drill.

Introduction:
Last term we learned many important English topics. Today we will revise what we know to strengthen our skills.

Content:
We will start with reading warm up. Read this passage about market day in Lagos carefully. Now write three sentences about what happens at your local market. Next we do grammar drill. Identify the nouns in these sentences: The teacher bought chalk for her class. The pupils wrote in their notebooks. Remember nouns are names of people, places or things.

Class activity:
In pairs, take turns reading a short paragraph from your textbook. Your partner will identify all the verbs in the paragraph.

Evaluation questions:
What is a noun?
Give an example of a verb.
Write a sentence about your school using three different nouns.

Summary:
Today we revised primary five English work through reading and writing activities.

topics.title: Comprehension: discipline
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to read and answer comprehension questions.
The pupils should be able to identify new words from the passage.

Introduction:
Last week we revised our English work. Today we will read a passage about discipline and answer questions about it.

Content:
Read this passage about discipline in schools carefully. Discipline means following rules and behaving well. After reading, answer these questions: What is discipline? Why is discipline important in school? Find these words in the passage: obedient, respect, responsibility. Use each word in your own sentence. For example, An obedient pupil follows teacher's instructions.

Class activity:
In groups, discuss a time when discipline helped you in school. Write three key points from your discussion.

Evaluation questions:
What does discipline mean?
Why is discipline important in the classroom?
Use the word 'respect' in a sentence.

Summary:
Today we practiced comprehension by reading about discipline and learning new words.

topics.title: Grammar: parts of speech review
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.
The pupils should be able to find parts of speech in given passages.

Introduction:
We have learned about different types of words in English. Today we will review nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.

Content:
A noun is a word for a person, place or thing like 'teacher', 'Lagos' or 'book'. A verb is an action word like 'run', 'write' or 'learn'. An adjective describes a noun like 'happy', 'big' or 'red'. An adverb describes a verb like 'quickly', 'well' or 'loudly'. Look at this sentence: The tall girl quickly ran to the market. Identify the noun (girl), adjective (tall), verb (ran) and adverb (quickly).

Class activity:
In pairs, take turns reading sentences from your textbook. Your partner will identify one noun, one verb, one adjective and one adverb in each sentence.

Evaluation questions:
What is a noun?
Give an example of an adjective.
Find the verb in this sentence: The children played football happily.

Summary:
Today we reviewed the four main parts of speech and practiced identifying them in sentences.

topics.title: Grammar: tenses
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify simple past and present perfect tenses.
The pupils should be able to change sentences between these tenses.

Introduction:
We have learned about different verb tenses. Today we will focus on simple past and present perfect tenses.

Content:
Simple past tense shows actions that happened before now. For example: I went to school yesterday. Present perfect tense shows actions that started in the past and continue now or have a result now. For example: I have finished my homework. To change from simple past to present perfect, use 'have' or 'has' with the past participle. Change 'She cooked jollof rice' to 'She has cooked jollof rice'.

Class activity:
Write five sentences about your weekend using simple past tense. Then change each sentence to present perfect tense.

Evaluation questions:
What is simple past tense?
What is present perfect tense?
Change this sentence to present perfect: They visited the museum last week.

Summary:
Today we learned how to identify and use simple past and present perfect tenses.

topics.title: Vocabulary: word families
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify root words with prefixes and suffixes.
The pupils should be able to build new words using root words.

Introduction:
We have learned about different types of words. Today we will learn how to build new words using root words with prefixes and suffixes.

Content:
A root word is the base word. A prefix is added to the beginning like 'un - ' or 're - '. A suffix is added to the end like ' - ing' or ' - ly'. For example, from 'happy' we can make 'unhappy' (prefix), 'happily' (suffix) or 'unhappily' (prefix and suffix). In Nigerian markets, you might see 'unripe' mangoes or 'freshly' ground pepper. These are all word families built from root words.

Class activity:
In groups, choose a root word like 'care' or 'play'. Build as many new words as possible using prefixes and suffixes. Share your best word with the class.

Evaluation questions:
What is a root word?
Give an example of a prefix.
Build a new word from 'friend' using a suffix.

Summary:
Today we learned how to build new words by adding prefixes and suffixes to root words.

topics.title: Composition: argument essay
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to plan an argument essay.
The pupils should be able to write an argument essay on whether children should use phones.

Introduction:
We have learned different types of compositions. Today we will write an argument essay about whether children should use phones.

Content:
An argument essay has introduction, points for, points against and conclusion. Introduction: Should children use phones? Points for: phones help with learning, can contact parents in emergency, educational apps available. Points against: phones can be distraction, expensive to buy and maintain, some content not suitable for children. Conclusion: Give your opinion based on the points. Remember to use linking words like 'however', 'furthermore' and 'in conclusion'.

Class activity:
In groups, make a list of three points for and three points against children using phones. Then write one paragraph using these points.

Evaluation questions:
What are the three parts of an argument essay?
Give one reason why children should use phones.
Give one reason why children should not use phones.

Summary:
Today we learned how to plan and write an argument essay about children using phones.

topics.title: Letter writing: formal
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify the features of a formal letter.
The pupils should be able to write a formal letter to the head teacher.

Introduction:
We have learned different types of letters. Today we will learn how to write a formal letter to the head teacher.

Content:
A formal letter has specific features: your address at top right, date below address, head teacher's address on left, subject line, formal greeting like 'Dear Sir/Ma', polite language, proper closing like 'Yours faithfully' and your signature. When writing to the head teacher, use respectful language. For example: I am writing to request permission to participate in the upcoming debate competition. I believe this will improve my public speaking skills.

Class activity:
Write a formal letter to your head teacher requesting permission to start a school gardening club. Include all the features we discussed.

Evaluation questions:
What is the proper closing for a formal letter to a head teacher?
Where does the head teacher's address go in a formal letter?
Write one sentence you would include in a formal letter to your head teacher.

Summary:
Today we learned the features of formal letters and practiced writing to the head teacher.

topics.title: Oral English: diphthongs
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify and pronounce diphthongs correctly.
The pupils should be able to practice diphthong sounds in words.

Introduction:
We have learned different sounds in English. Today we will practice diphthong sounds which are two vowel sounds together.

Content:
Diphthongs are two vowel sounds in one syllable. We will practice 'oi' as in 'coin' and 'oil', 'ou' as in 'out' and 'house', and 'ie' as in 'pie' and 'field'. In Nigerian English, these sounds might sound different from British English. For example, when saying 'coin', your mouth moves from 'o' to 'i' sound. Practice saying these words: oil, house, field, noise, flower.

Class activity:
In pairs, take turns saying words with diphthongs. Your partner will check if you are pronouncing them correctly. Then say this sentence: The noisy boys found oil in the field.

Evaluation questions:
What is a diphthong?
Give a word with the 'oi' sound.
Say this word: 'house'

Summary:
Today we practiced identifying and pronouncing diphthong sounds in English words.

topics.title: Literature: poem study
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to read and discuss a Nigerian poem.
The pupils should be able to identify figures of speech in the poem.

Introduction:
We have read different types of literature. Today we will study a Nigerian poem and learn about figures of speech.

Content:
Read this poem about harmattan season in Nigeria. Harmattan brings cold, dry wind and dust from the north. Figures of speech make language interesting. Simile compares using 'like' or 'as': The harmattan wind is as strong as a lion. Metaphor says something is something else: The harmattan is a giant breathing dust. Personification gives human qualities to things: The harmattan whispers through the trees. Find these in the poem and discuss what they mean.

Class activity:
In groups, write a short poem about your favorite Nigerian food using at least two figures of speech. Share your poem with the class.

Evaluation questions:
What is a simile?
Give an example of a metaphor from the poem.
What does personification mean?

Summary:
Today we read a Nigerian poem and identified different figures of speech used in it.

topics.title: Revision and assessment
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to recall term's topics.
The pupils should be able to complete a class test on term's work.

Introduction:
This week we will revise all we have learned this term and take a test to show what we know.

Content:
We have covered many topics this term: comprehension, grammar parts of speech, tenses, vocabulary, argument essays, formal letters, diphthongs and Nigerian poetry. Review your notes on each topic. Pay special attention to tenses and parts of speech as these are very important. In the test, you will answer questions on all these topics to show your understanding.

Class activity:
In pairs, ask each other questions about the topics we have covered this term. Take turns being the teacher and the pupil.

Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between simple past and present perfect tense?
Name two figures of speech we learned.
What are the features of a formal letter?

Summary:
Today we revised all term's topics and prepared for our end of term assessment.
